definition: Combining the positions reported by several surveillance systems into one best estimate for each aircraft, weighted by how accurate each system is.
The system's running estimate of one aircraft: its position, speed, direction, altitude and identity, updated whenever a sensor reports it.
When no fresh data arrives, a track keeps moving along its predicted path for a short time and is marked as coasting, before it is dropped.
An automatic check that warns the controller or pilot when something is about to go wrong, as a last line of defence.
A ground safety net that warns the controller when two aircraft are predicted to come too close within the next minute or two.
A ground safety net that warns the controller when an aircraft is, or soon will be, too close to the terrain below it.
An on-board system with a terrain map that warns the pilots, for example with "TERRAIN, PULL UP", before the aircraft gets too close to the ground.
When one part of a system fails, the whole keeps working in a reduced but safe way instead of stopping completely.
Keeping aircraft apart using position reports, times and levels instead of a live surveillance picture, with larger safety distances.
Airspace over the ocean, far from ground radar and VHF radio, where aircraft rely on satellite links, HF radio and position reports.
The minimum distance aircraft must keep from each other, sideways (for example 3 or 5 NM) or vertically (usually 1,000 ft).
